items.title: docs(readme): re-measure the whole benchmark table
items.body:
Every row re-measured on one host, release build, `--repeat 5` medians, using the commands the README documents. DOOP keeps `--repeat 1` for the reason its footnote already gives.

The W>1 DOOP numbers depend on the #959 fix (`fac34fa`), already on main.

## Four tuple counts fell, and the new ones are correct

| workload | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| DDISASM | 900 | **704** |
| Polonius | 1,999 | **1,983** |
| CRDT | 2,156,530 | **2,152,328** |
| DOOP | 14,096,448 | **13,828,835** |

Iteration counts are unchanged throughout.

**Cause: `059e410` (#957)** — a single-rule relation was not deduplicated, so a head projecting away a body variable derived one row per *derivation* instead of one per distinct tuple. Datalog is set-valued, so the old totals were counting duplicates.

**Bisected, not assumed.** Building both sides of that commit on this host:

```
059e410^   ddisasm=900  polonius=1999  crdt=2156530   <- the previous table, exactly
059e410    ddisasm=704  polonius=1983  crdt=2152328   <- this table, exactly
```

DOOP is attributed by consistency rather than a two-sided build — 23 minutes a run makes that expensive — and the footnote says so rather than implying it was measured.

That also retires a claim the old footnote made: it stated 14,096,448 was **already** a post-#957 figure. It was not, and re-measurement does not reproduce it.

## DOOP's FAIL columns become numbers

All three widths now agree on 13,828,835 tuples and 153 iterations. Agreement across widths is the property worth recording — an earlier revision explicitly could not claim it (#958).

Scaling is weak, **1.20x at W=8 and 1.23x at W=16**, and the footnote states that plainly rather than letting the wall-clock column imply a speedup story.

The footnote also drops its old explanation of the failure — "the session cap divided by the worker count" — because that was wrong. The divisor was the K-fusion *branch* count applied to the whole session budget, so capacity shrank with the branch fan, not the width.

## Timing movement elsewhere

Descriptive host noise, not called out row by row, per the paragraph already in the README that says so. The one row that moved materially is **CSPA at W=1, 1.32s → 1.59s**. It is the largest non-DOOP workload and the most host-sensitive, and nothing in this range is being read as an algorithmic change.

## Note

Degraded sequential mode (subagent limit reached). The measurements are the substance here and they are reproducible from the documented commands; the bisection above is what I would want a reviewer to spot-check first.

## Intent Publish the project's benchmark results: (1) a cross-engine 'Benchmarks' table in the main README showing, per query class, where MySQL 5.7 workloads regress or improve on each migration candidate (5.7→8.0 and 5.7→MariaDB 10.11, Δp95 plus Δmean where the source reports emphasize it), with regressions visually distinct via plain-text-friendly markers (bold + sign, not color-only); (2) the three executed benchmark writeups ported into docs/benchmarks/ (2026-07-16-mysql80-general.md, 2026-07-16-mysql80-hugetext.md, 2026-07-16-mariadb.md) and linked from the table and from docs/quickstart.md. The writeups are faithful ports of internal executed reports, scrubbed of internal references; every number was transcribed exactly from the source reports and verified — numeric values in the table and writeups are ground truth from real runs and must not be 'corrected'. Required footnotes kept deliberately: the 8.0 general run was stock-charset (charset confound deliberate — baselines labeled latin1-5.7 vs utf8mb4-5.7); blob MB/s absolutes are not comparable across tool versions (sql-replay 0.2.0 vs 0.4.0 memory model); all numbers are WSL2 ratios, not production absolutes; MariaDB sql_mode behavioral diffs called out as the real migration gotcha. The story the table tells: 8.0's group-by/temp-table cliff (up to ~5x, tunable) vs MariaDB's -15% on the same class; blob transfer at par on both; per-statement overhead on tiny queries as 8.0's other loss. A prior run raised the ask-user finding 'quickstart-charset-alone-overclaim' about docs/quickstart.md; the user decided: attribute the ~5x GROUP BY slowdown to stock 8.0 defaults (utf8mb4 default + TempTable on-disk spill), NOT 'charset alone' and NOT 'largely charset-driven' — that decided fix is already applied as the branch's pipeline fix commit 4e8e2c3 (no-mistakes(review): reword quickstart GROUP BY slowdown attribution to stock defaults); the finding is resolved and must not re-surface. items.title: Simplify the docs and fix what they got wrong
items.body:
Cuts ~750 lines from `doc/` and corrects a set of statements that were wrong against the code.

## Why the docs were long

Nearly every guide opened with a large ASCII diagram, followed immediately by a numbered list restating the same steps in prose. `12_image_processing_pipeline.md` had seven diagram boxes above seven numbered paragraphs with the same seven titles. That pattern accounted for most of the length.

## What happened to the diagrams

Kept, where they show something prose cannot:

- **Request lifecycle** – redrawn compactly around the one genuinely non-linear part, the cache short-circuit, with the error exits on the branches that produce them.
- **Introduction** – a topology sketch (users → CDN → imgforge → origin), which is the thing a block of text is bad at.
- **Prometheus** – where each metric fires during a request, which the metrics table does not convey.
- **Pipeline** – a one-line stage chain instead of a full-page box diagram.
- **URL anatomy** – a real URL with the segments labelled underneath, replacing three tables of box art.

Dropped: the caching fan-out (four backends each pointing at "HIT/MISS"), whose only real content was a comparison table drawn in box characters — now a markdown table.

## Corrections

Each verified against the source, not assumed:

| Doc said | Actually |
| --- | --- |
| `gravity:center`, `watermark:0.7:south_east` in examples | Only two-letter anchors parse (`ce`, `soea`, …). Both fall through to centre **silently** — the watermark examples produced a centred watermark with no error. |
| Missing/invalid bearer token → `401` | `403`. imgforge never returns `401`. |
| Changing a preset definition invalidates its cached entries | It does not. The cache key is the path as written, so `pr:thumbnail` keeps serving the old rendering until eviction. This is now documented as the reason to version preset names. |
| `format` defaults to `jpeg` | Defaults to the source format since 0.12.0. The quick-reference row still had the old behaviour. |
| `IMGFORGE_CACHE_MODE`, `IMGFORGE_PORT` | Neither exists. `IMGFORGE_CACHE_TYPE` and `IMGFORGE_BIND`. |
| `nearest` is ~6x faster than `lanczos3` | See below. |

Also fixed: links to `2_quick_start.md` and `11_contributing.md` (neither exists), a malformed vegeta URL, a Foyer link pointing at an unrelated project, a `docker run` snippet missing a line continuation, and another passing `--help` in the step that claims to start the server.

## The benchmark tables in 5.1

`5.1_resizing_algorithms.md` (340 lines for a five-value enum) carried per-kernel millisecond figures and speed ratios. They were invented, and the ratios were wrong by an order of magnitude — libvips shrinks in stages before the kernel runs, so on a 4000×3000 → 800×600 downscale the five kernels land within noise of one another, not the claimed 6× spread. `nearest` measured *slower* than `lanczos3` from a JPEG source.

The advice built on those numbers ("use `linear` for thumbnails, it's 3× faster") was therefore steering people toward worse-looking images for no gain. Committing straight to `stage` meant unreviewed work was in front of four people the moment it was pushed. This makes `stage` an integration branch that only ever receives merges.

```
<type>/<thing>  →  stage  →  main
```

- Conventional branch types: `feat/`, `fix/`, `refactor/`, `test/`, `docs/`, `chore/`.
- `--no-ff` merges, so a branch reads as one unit of work in the history.
- `stage` → `main` at block boundaries only, green, announced.

items.title: Actually verify the DKIM signature; fix stale docs; add security policy
items.body:
## The DKIM signature had never been verified

```go
verifications, err := dkim.Verify(...)
if err != nil {
    // Verification might fail because we don't have real DNS
    // ... (empty block)
}
_ = verifications          // discarded
// t.Errorf(...)           // the only real assertion, commented out
```

All it asserted was that the string `DKIM-Signature:` appeared. **A structurally plausible but cryptographically wrong signature would have passed.**

That's worse than it sounds — receivers treat a *failed* signature as a stronger negative than no signature at all, and the failure is silent: you find out from a deliverability dashboard, not an error.

And it was always closable offline:

```go
type VerifyOptions struct {
    LookupTXT func(domain string) ([]string, error)   // ← stub the DNS
}
```

**12 tests** now run a real verifier over signed output: both canonicalisations, multipart with attachments, Unicode subject and body, and header coverage.

The **negative controls** are what make the rest mean anything:

- a tampered body, subject or `From` must fail to verify
- a signature must not verify against a key that didn't produce it

Both hold. **The signing was correct all along** — it's proven now rather than assumed. Less dramatic than finding a bug, but it's the outcome that matters for a deliverability-critical feature.

## The README documented removed APIs

`v0.8.0` removed `ValidateEmailExistence` and the `gsmail.MSO*` aliases, and the README still told people to call them — so copying from it produced code that doesn't compile. My fault: I updated the sections I touched and didn't sweep the rest.

All **41** exported symbols the README references now resolve (checked mechanically). The benchmark table also quoted `BenchmarkHasHeader`, which no longer exists, and stale figures; replaced with current ones plus a note to run them yourself.

## Security policy and dependency automation

`SECURITY.md` — private reporting, and more usefully a statement of what the library **does and does not** defend against, so a report can be judged against a stated boundary. Header injection, untrusted MIME bounds, generated HTML, webhook authentication and credential handling are in scope; content you pass in, delivery guarantees and `InsecureSkipVerify` are explicitly not.

`.github/dependabot.yml` — ten CVEs were found by hand in one review. `govulncheck` catches reachable ones per push, but nothing kept dependencies current between reviews. Grouped by AWS / OpenTelemetry / `golang.org/x` so it's one PR a week, not a dozen.

items.body:
Adds the reproducible incident benchmark and the evaluation harness that produces the paper's numbers.

## Benchmark (N=6)
Each scenario is a `model -> tool -> model` agent with three tool variants (ungated incident / gated fix / benign unrelated change) and a `safe()` invariant the cut-point test asserts:

| Scenario | Failure class |
|---|---|
| Refund / Invoice / Trade | argument-confusion tool-safety bugs (now with benign variant + `safe()`) |
| Email blast | over-broad action / wrong audience scope (new) |
| Payout injection | prompt injection into a tool arg + allowlist verification (new) |
| Prod delete | destructive action without an environment gate (new) |

## Harness (`examples/benchmark/harness.py`)
Records each incident and measures, over all six:

- **Recording overhead** (in-memory, isolates compute from disk): ~20 µs/crossing = **0.007%** of a 300 ms model call.
- **Store growth**: ≤ **1.44 KB/crossing**.
- **Replay**: full-stub replay is deterministic (20 replays each) with **0 live (model) crossings**.

items.title: docs: let tables wrap instead of silently clipping at max-content
items.body:
## Problem

`docs/style.css` forced every table to `width: max-content` with `white-space: nowrap` headers. This disables the browser's normal table shrink-to-fit, and the overflow spills into Mintlify's scroll wrapper — which hides its scrollbar (`scrollbar-width: none`) and paints no edge fade. Net effect: **wide tables render as content silently cut off at the right edge**, with no cue that more columns exist. The rule was presumably meant to make wide tables scrollable, but Mintlify already wraps every table in its own scroll area, so the table's own `overflow-x: auto` never triggers — the rule only delivered the harmful side effect (no wrapping), not the intended one.

Audited all **178 tables across the 70 nav pages** with headless Chrome at 1280/1440 viewports: **34 tables were clipping**, some hiding entire columns or 2000+px of prose. After this change every table wraps to fit; the one table whose min-content genuinely exceeds the content column degrades to the built-in horizontal scroll automatically.

## Fix

- Drop `display: block / overflow-x / width: max-content` from `table` and `white-space: nowrap` from `th` — restore normal table layout so columns wrap to the available width.
- Zero out Mintlify's `[&_td]:min-w-[150px]` floor (`th, td { min-width: 0 }`), which alone forces a 9-column table to ≥1350px against a ~719px content column.

No per-table markup or opt-outs needed: whether a table wraps or scrolls is decided by the browser per table (wraps when it can, scrolls only when its minimum width physically exceeds the column).

## Examples (1440px viewport; before = live site, after = this PR)

The 8-column comparison table showed only its first column-and-a-half; 452px hidden.

items.title: docs: rewrite all prose to ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English
items.body:
Rewrites all hand-written prose in the repo to [ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Technical_English), and adds the style guide that makes STE the standard.

Every file went through three passes: the humanizer skill, the unslop skill, then a rewrite to STE.

## The three commits

| Commit | Scope | Files |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| `docs(style)` | New prose style guide; the five existing guides rewritten to match | 7 |
| `docs` | Hand-written Markdown: root docs, 60 crate READMEs, website content | 83 |
| `docs` | `///` and `//!` comments across 70 crates, about 82,600 doc lines | 1615 |

Review the first commit on its own. It is short, and it defines the rules the other two apply.

## Verification

Checked across all 2284 in-scope `.rs` files and all 88 in-scope Markdown files:

- No line outside a `///` or `//!` comment changed.
- No intra-doc link was removed. No heading, code fence, or link target changed in Markdown.
- Every doctest fence is byte-identical, in all 75 files that have one.
- No generated file was edited. The 466 files under `crates/protocol/generated` and the protobuf-derived files carry a generated marker and were skipped.
- No negation or scope word was weakened. Crypto constants, metric names, `SQLSTATE` codes, `KIP-###` references, OIDs, and measured figures are unchanged.
- `cargo doc --no-deps --workspace` reports the same 44 warnings as before the pass.
- The codegen snapshot tests, the docgen tests, and every doctest pass.

## Two rules worth knowing

**`must` against `should`.** STE writes `must` for a requirement. A first pass over-applied that and converted 71 advisory statements. A repair pass reviewed all 71 against the code: 55 went back to `should`, and 16 kept `must` because an `Err` return, a panic, an assert, or a protocol rejection enforces them. The style guide now states this rule, because it changes what an API promises.

**No boilerplate `# Errors` or `# Panics`.** A section must state the real conditions for its own item.

## What this does not fix

The rewrite surfaced defects that need an owner, not a rewording. Every one was left verbatim:

- **Eight boilerplate `# Errors` and `# Panics` strings, copied hundreds of times, many false.** A `# Panics` body names a poisoned mutex in a file with no mutex. A `# Errors` body names Kubernetes in a crate with no Kubernetes dependency. Encode functions are documented as failing on truncated input. `gres-substrate/src/stats.rs::publish` documents an error type that does not exist, because its `Result` error is the rejected snapshot.
- **`pgexec` depth constants.** `agg::MAX_GROUPED_DEPTH` is 150 and its doc claims it mirrors `eval::MAX_EVAL_DEPTH`, which is 100. `eval.rs` records that 150 caused an aborting stack overflow three times. Worth an owner's eye.
- **Website contradictions.** The broker count is three in two files and six in three others. The homepage memory figures do not match the benchmark table. Both live in TOML front matter and were not touched.
- Doc comments spliced across items in eight crates, two broken intra-doc links in `gres-loadtest`, an empty heading at `crates/broker/tests/KNOWN_ISSUES.md:40`, and an `assert_eq!` in `crates/verified/src/offset_allocator.rs` that `CLAUDE.md` forbids.
- **A rule conflict between two normative files.** `docs/style_guides/code_style_guide.md` permits a narrowly-scoped `#[allow(...)]` with a reason. `CLAUDE.md` forbids every Clippy suppression. They need to agree.

## Out of scope

Everything under `docs/` except the style guides, plus `docs/superpowers/`, `crates/gres-conformance/`, the compatibility matrices, the release-plz CHANGELOGs, the vendored adidoks theme, `STATUS.md`, and `docs/configuration-audit.md`.

items.title: fix(docs): correct seven stale component counts, guard the class in CI
items.body:
## What

Fixes seven stale component counts that are shipping right now, then makes the class mechanically impossible to reintroduce.

| # | File:line | Said | Should be |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `AGENTS.md:33` | 11 reusable agent templates | 12 |
| 2 | `AGENTS.md:34` | 18 reusable skill templates | 19 |
| 3 | `README.md:97` | "We give you **11**" | 12 |
| 4 | `i18n/README.ja.md:107` | `**11個**` | 12 |
| 5 | `i18n/README.ko.md:107` | `**11개**` | 12 |
| 6 | `i18n/README.zh.md:107` | `**11 个**` | 12 |
| 7 | `docs/SETTINGS-GUIDE.md:292` | 8 lifecycle events | 9 |

Rows 3 to 6 are one bug replicated in four languages. That is the case worth automating: a contributor who fixes the English line has three translated copies to remember, in scripts they may not read.

`AGENTS.md` is the first file an AI assistant reads to orient itself in the repo, so a wrong count there is wrong at the point of maximum leverage.

## Why a CI guard, and why now

Stale counts have been corrected four separate times in this release cycle: the visual assets, `setup.sh`, the "43 automated tests" figure, and now these seven. Each fix was a manual sweep, and each missed some. `tests/count-check.sh` derives every expected value from the filesystem and asserts that each published copy agrees.

Adding a thirteenth agent now fails **17 bindings across 13 files** and names every one, which is the checklist a contributor previously had to reconstruct by hand.

## Why a registry rather than a prose sweep

The obvious design is to scan prose for `<digit> <category>` and compare. I built that first and measured it. It produced **7 false positives and missed 4 real bugs**:

- **False positives**, all legitimate text: per-preset deltas (`Add 4 hooks + 2 agents`), adoption rows (`CLAUDE.md + 2 hooks`), and card markup where three whole cards share one line so "the number nearest the label" is a coin flip.
- **Misses**, all real: `11 reusable agent templates` (an adjective splits the digit from the category), a bare `**11**` whose category is in the previous clause, and the three CJK counter forms where the category sits in another clause and another script.

`SETUP.md` settles the question: `+ 4 more hooks, 2 agents` and `+ all 12 agents, 19 skills` sit one line apart in the same table. Totals and deltas are not lexically separable, so no amount of regex tuning fixes the sweep.

So the guard registers what is right instead of excluding what is wrong: an explicit `(file, anchor, expected)` binding per published total, with every expected value derived from the filesystem.

**Trade-off, stated plainly:** a registry cannot catch a count introduced in a brand-new location tomorrow, which a sweep theoretically could. But the sweep's measured behavior was 11 wrong verdicts out of 13, so its theoretical reach bought nothing. When you add a new published count, add a binding. A `MISSING_ANCHOR` failure is how the guard tells you a document was reworded out from under it, rather than silently checking nothing.

**Bindings are per-line, not per-file, because a file is not a trust boundary.** `i18n/README.ko.md` states our agent count on line 107 and Project-AI-MemoryCore's "11 feature extensions" on line 303, in the same CJK counter form. A file-level rule would either miss the bug or corrupt a third-party credit. Anchors bind to surrounding text, so they cannot drift onto the wrong line.

## CI wiring

Only the `push` trigger is widened (to include `**/*.md` and `assets/**`). The `pull_request` trigger deliberately keeps **no path filter**, per the existing comment: a required check that is skipped on some PRs would block their merge forever.

## Verification

- Guard run on the **unfixed** tree: failed with exactly the 7 findings above and no false positives. A guard that passes on a known-broken tree is measuring nothing.
- Guard after the fixes: **56 pass / 0 fail**.
- Adversarial: added a 13th agent (17 bindings fail across 13 files), a 20th skill, a 7th rule, and a 22nd battle story; each was caught and each reverted cleanly to green.
- False-positive pass: preset deltas, adoption rows, `up to 4 agents`, Cursor's `~11 hook types`, the benchmark tables, `minimal 3-file setup`, and the 4/10/20/55 preset file counts are all untouched and unflagged.
- `hooks/test-hooks.sh`: still exactly **55 pass / 0 fail**, proving the guard did not inflate the very number it asserts.
- `tests/install-matrix.sh`: **19 passed / 0 failed**.
- Portability: passes under `LC_ALL=C` (the CJK anchors are locale-independent) and when invoked from an arbitrary working directory. No `python`, `jq`, or `node` dependency in executed code. LF line endings, enforced by the existing `.gitattributes`.

Two rounds of adversarial review were run against the guard itself, and both found real defects that are fixed here: unbound battle-story counts and an unbound `docs/WHY.md` tier line (dead ground truth that shipped the appearance of a check), a card matcher that silently skipped `assets/card-social-preview.html` entirely, a sum check that accepted `14 + 1 = 15` while both addends were wrong, and a missing ambiguity guard in `card()` that made a duplicated label resolve by document order.

items.title: feat(docs): overall benchmark summary table + combined trend plot
items.body:
## Summary

On top of #196 (per-suite grouped ratio tables, capped/date-labelled
columns, collapsed per-benchmark plots — closing #192/#193), this adds
the "overall" layer the maintainer asked for: the benchmarks page now
leads with a compact, skimmable summary before the detail — deliberately
terse, matching the tone of CensoredDistributions.jl's own PR-comparison
comment (`benchmark/comment/comment.jl`), not a multi-paragraph explainer.

**Page top (always visible):**
- `## Benchmark summary (overall)`: one row per suite — `Suite |
  Median ratio | Trend | Status`. Ratio is the suite's median benchmark
  value at the most recent shown revision against its value at the
  oldest shown revision (1.00 = no change). Trend is an arrow (↗/→/↘)
  past a 2% threshold; Status flags `⚠ reg` at/above
  `HISTORY_REGRESSION_THRESHOLD` (default 1.1 = 10%). One caption line,
  not a paragraph.
- One combined trend plot (`overall_trend.png`): all suites as series
  over the last `HISTORY_COMMITS` commits. Regenerated on every docs
  build straight from `table.md` (like `index.md`/the API pages) via a
  lazily loaded `Plots` (GR backend) — no CI workflow change needed.
  Missing dependency or <2 comparable revisions degrades to the table
  only, with an `@info`/`@warn` note, never fails the build.
- **New:** `### Skipped & broken benchmarks` — a package-owned,
  write-once notes hook (`docs/benchmarks_notes.md`, same lifecycle as
  the narrative prose hook, seeded with a placeholder) for hand-written
  notes on why a suite is excluded or a scenario is known-broken. Any
  benchmark with no parseable data across the shown revisions is
  auto-appended alongside it.

**Collapsed below**, inside one `<details>`: the existing #196 per-suite
ratio tables and per-benchmark plot wall.

New `HISTORY_REGRESSION_THRESHOLD` config const (managed template +
`build_docs`/`build_benchmark_page` kwarg), following the same `_cfg`
graceful-default pattern as `HISTORY_COMMITS`/`HISTORY_SUITES`.

The kit's own `docs/docs_config.jl` keeps `BENCHMARK_PAGE = false` (no
benchmark suite of its own — intentional, unchanged); `docs/make.jl` was
re-synced via `scaffold_update(".")`.

Closes #202

## Independent review fixes

An independent fresh-context review of the first commit found real bugs,
all fixed here:
- `_suite_column_medians` silently misaligned a malformed row's stale,
  uncapped values with the newest (capped) revision columns instead of
  skipping it entirely — fed straight into the headline ratio/trend/
  status. Fixed + regression test.
- No dependency-provisioning path for the trend plot's `Plots` dep on
  scaffold: added `benchmarks`-gated deps/compat to
  `templates/docs/Project.toml` (`_bench_docs_deps`, mirroring
  `_ad_docs_deps`). Scaffold-time only — an already-scaffolded package's
  package-owned `docs/Project.toml` needs it added by hand (called out
  in the docstring).
- A zero/degenerate baseline could produce NaN/Inf ratios that silently
  passed the threshold comparisons as "no change" instead of "n/a".
  Guarded the baseline pick (skip zero) and tightened the finite-value
  filter (defence in depth); `_fmt_ratio` never prints a literal
  "NaN"/"Inf".
- The plot-render `try`/`catch` conflated "Plots not installed"
  (expected, `@info`) with a genuine render failure (now `@warn`, with
  a dedicated test forcing the failure path).
- The detail section re-parsed `table.md` and re-shelled out to `git
  show` a second time for the same data the summary had just computed;
  now reuses the already-reshaped `(col_labels, groups)`.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests: `_parse_metric_value`, `_suite_column_medians`
      (including the malformed-row-width fix), `_suite_ratio_series`
      (including zero-baseline), `_suite_trend_status` (trend arrows,
      regression flag + boundary, NaN defence-in-depth,
      insufficient-data case), `_write_benchmark_summary`,
      `_write_benchmark_notes`, `_unparsed_benchmarks`, `_fmt_ratio`.
- [x] Integration tests via `build_benchmark_page` (git-backed, real
      `table.md` fixtures): overall summary leads the page above the
      collapsed detail; correct ratio/trend/status per suite
      (regression/improvement/flat); `overall_trend.png` generated +
      embedded; single-revision case skips the plot cleanly (no `Plots`
      invocation); notes block renders user prose + auto-detected
      no-data benchmarks; plot render-failure path hits the `@warn`
      branch and degrades to `false`.
- [x] Scaffold-level test: `docs/benchmarks_notes.md` is seeded on
      `scaffold(...; benchmarks=true)`, absent when `benchmarks=false`,
      and round-trips a hand edit unchanged through `scaffold_update`.
- [x] Full kit suite green: `Pkg.test(test_args=["skip_quality"])` —
      1461 passed, 7 pre-existing broken, 0 failures.
- [x] QA suite green: Aqua, ExplicitImports, import centralisation,
      docstring format, README sections, doctest, formatting, JET
      (fixed a JET-flagged type instability along the way: read
      `m.match` instead of `m.captures[1]`, which is typed
      `Union{Nothing,SubString}` even for a non-optional capture group).
- [x] `JuliaFormatter` clean (`task format`), no line > 80 chars in
      Julia source, no trailing whitespace.
- [x] `scaffold_update(".")` on the kit itself: only `docs/make.jl`
      changed (mirrors the template edit exactly), idempotent on a
      second run — zero drift. `docs/benchmarks_notes.md` correctly

The status block said *"verified against one commercial title"* while the benchmark table three sections below it lists rows for both Mario Kart 8 and Breath of the Wild — the README contradicted itself. Now names both titles, and names the machine: an **8 GB M2 Mac mini**, macOS 26.5.

spin:  mean 182.9%  median 183.5%  (162.2-202.9) of one core
park:  mean  97.6%  median 103.9%  ( 70.1-115.8)

items.title: Release v0.1.4 — version bump + license-header fix
items.body:
Cuts the **0.1.4** artifact version for the benchmark-documentation release and fixes a license-header regression on the generated `index.html`.

## Version bump 0.1.3 → 0.1.4

No appender code changed — this release ships the reproducible 2026-08-04 CloudHub benchmark (merged in #1) under a clean, versioned tag.

- `versions:set` across the reactor: parent + `batch-http-core`, `batch-http-log4j2`, `demo/java/benchmark`.
- `batchhttp.version` property in the two Mule demo apps.
- README: build-instructions version, dependency-snippet version, and a `v0.1.4` changelog entry.

The benchmark tables and `index.html` **keep the `0.1.3` label on purpose** — that is the build that was measured. Bumping them would falsely claim the benchmark ran on 0.1.4.

## Fix: license header on generated index.html

The data-driven `generate_report_html.py` emitted the Apache-2.0 license header and a "GENERATED FILE" note inside a **single** HTML comment. `license-maven-plugin` (which checks `docs/index.html`) extracts the whole comment and compares it to the expected header, so the extra note made it report the header as missing — failing `mvn validate` / `license:check`.

This regression was introduced in #1 (the original hand-written `index.html` had a clean header). Fixed by splitting the generated-file note into its own comment block after the license header, then regenerating. Only the comment structure changed — no report content or numbers moved.

## Validation

- `mvn license:check` → **BUILD SUCCESS**; `mvn validate` → clean.
- `index.html` diff vs `main` is header-only; all headline numbers (55.5× / 133.8× / 7.6× / 55.9× and the per-app req/s) intact.
- No hidden files/folders touched.

items.title: fix: query parameter bugs, benchmark harness, crate metadata (v0.2.4)
items.body:
## Summary

Three query-parameter bugs found while building a reproducible benchmark harness, the harness itself, and crates.io metadata for all nine crates. Bumps the workspace version to 0.2.4.

## Bug fixes (`postrust-core`)

| Bug | Symptom | Fix |
|-----|---------|-----|
| `limit`/`offset` ignored | Parsed into `QueryParams::ranges`, which was read nowhere — every request returned the entire table | Resolved into the read plan, taking precedence over the `Range` header as in PostgREST |
| Filters failed on non-text columns | `?id=eq.42` → `400 PGRST504`, PostgreSQL reporting `operator does not exist: integer = text` | Placeholder carries an explicit cast, using the column's `udt_name` (`information_schema` reports arrays as `ARRAY` and enums as `USER-DEFINED`, neither castable) |
| Negated filters generated invalid SQL | `col NOT = $1` only parses for operators like `LIKE`/`IN`, so `?id=not.eq.4` returned a 400 | Comparison parenthesised as `NOT (col = $1)` |

Cast injection is guarded by `castable_type`, which accepts only bare type names, with unit tests.

## Tests

New `crates/postrust-server/tests/query_params.rs` — 26 tests driving the real router in-process against a live database: `select`, `limit`, `offset`, `order`, `Range` header (including `limit` precedence), filters across integer/text/boolean/numeric/jsonb, `in`, `is.null`, negation, combined queries, and a SQL-injection check.

Marked `#[ignore]` per the existing convention so `cargo test` passes without a database; CI already runs `-- --ignored`, and `scripts/test.sh` now loads the fixtures and runs them locally too.

All 26 pass. Full workspace green, clippy clean, website type-checks.

## Benchmark harness

`scripts/bench.sh` + `scripts/bench-fixtures.sql`: builds the release binary, starts a throwaway PostgreSQL container, loads 100k rows, verifies each scenario returns 2xx **before** timing it, reports size/latency/RSS, and tears everything down.

Two details worth noting: `ab` reports `Failed requests: 0` for uniform-length error bodies, so non-2xx is checked separately (this is exactly how the integer-filter bug hid — a benchmark of a 400 path looked healthy and fast); and waits use wall-clock deadlines rather than iteration counts.

## Documentation

Binary size was previously stated as `~3.5 MB` on the website and `~5 MB` in the README. Both were measuring real builds of **different feature sets**:

| Build | Size |
|-------|------|
| default features | 3,070,080 bytes (2.93 MiB) |
| `--features admin-ui`, as shipped by the Dockerfile and CI | 5,220,864 bytes (4.98 MiB) |

Docs now state both with the feature set attached. Adds `docs/benchmarking.md`, a `/docs/benchmarks` website page, and benchmark tables in the README.

## Crate metadata

Every crate gains an expanded description, `homepage`, `keywords`, and a README whose crate table cross-links all nine crates to crates.io and docs.rs. New `/packages` page on the website, linked from the header and footer.

`categories` is deliberately omitted — an unrecognised slug is rejected by crates.io at publish time, which would break a release mid-flight.

## Release

Version bumped to 0.2.4 in `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`. Tag `v0.2.4` to be pushed after merge, so the release workflow's tag-vs-version guard checks against a `main` that contains it.
